overview: dbt sources and seeds are the two entry points for raw data in a dbt project: sources declare tables that already exist in the warehouse (loaded by an ingestion tool), while seeds are small static CSV files stored in the dbt repo that dbt loads into the warehouse for you.

Sources are referenced with {{ source('name','table') }} and declared in a YAML file (version: 2, sources: ...); this decouples model SQL from raw table names, makes the raw layer explicit in lineage, and enables freshness checks that warn when upstream data is stale.

Seeds live in the seeds/ folder, are loaded with 'dbt seed', and are referenced with {{ ref('seed_name') }} just like a model; they are ideal for small, version-controlled reference data (country codes, category mappings) but are never meant for large or frequently-changing data.
learningObjectives: Declare raw warehouse tables as dbt sources in a YAML file and reference them with {{ source('name','table') }}.
Configure and interpret source freshness checks (loaded_at_field, warn_after, error_after) and run 'dbt source freshness'.
Create and load seed CSV files with 'dbt seed', reference them via ref(), and decide correctly between a source and a seed.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: In dbt, a source is a named pointer to a set of tables that already exist in the target warehouse, declared under the top-level 'sources' key in a YAML file (version: 2) with a logical name, database, schema, and a list of tables; it is referenced in models with the {{ source('source_name', 'table_name') }} Jinja function, which resolves at compile time to the fully qualified relation and registers a dependency edge in the DAG. A seed is a CSV file placed in the project's seed-paths directory (default seeds/) that dbt materializes as a table in the warehouse when you run 'dbt seed'; it becomes a first-class node referenced with {{ ref('seed_name') }}. Sources represent externally loaded raw data; seeds represent small, static, version-controlled data that lives in the repository itself.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of your warehouse as a kitchen. Sources are the raw ingredients someone else already delivered and put in the fridge - dbt does not deliver them, it just writes a labeled note ('the raw orders are on this shelf') so your recipes can point to them by name and so you can check whether the milk has gone off (freshness). Seeds are little jars of pantry staples you keep in your own cupboard and version-control - like a small list mapping country codes to country names. You hand dbt the CSV, it puts the jar on the shelf with 'dbt seed', and your recipes reference it the same way they reference a cooked dish. Big deliveries go through sources; tiny handwritten lists you own go through seeds.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Sources were added to dbt in version 0.13 (2019) to give the raw layer an explicit, testable identity: before sources, models often selected directly from raw tables by hard-coded name, which broke lineage and environment portability. Source freshness checks arrived shortly after so teams could detect stale upstream loads (from Fivetran, Airbyte, custom loaders) before building models on top of them. Seeds have existed since dbt's early days as a simple way to version-control small lookup data alongside transformation code, reflecting dbt's philosophy that analytics logic - including reference data - belongs in git. Together they formalized the boundary between 'data loaded by others' and 'data owned by the analytics project'.

whyItMatters.business: Declaring sources and validating freshness means dashboards are built on data known to be current; a stale-load alert catches a broken ingestion pipeline before finance sees yesterday's numbers presented as today's, protecting trust in reporting.
whyItMatters.engineering: Sources decouple model SQL from physical raw table names, so re-pointing to a new schema or environment is a one-line YAML change instead of edits across dozens of models; seeds keep small reference data in version control so mappings are reviewed and reproducible rather than hand-edited in the warehouse.
whyItMatters.scalability: As a project grows to hundreds of models, a single source declaration is reused everywhere and appears once in lineage; seeds keep small lookups consistent across all environments without a separate load process, so the pattern scales cleanly.
whyItMatters.cost: Freshness checks let you skip or delay builds when upstream data has not changed, avoiding wasted warehouse compute; keeping seeds tiny avoids the cost and slowness of loading large data through a mechanism designed for kilobytes, not gigabytes.
whyItMatters.reliability: Explicit sources make the raw layer testable (freshness, not_null on raw columns) and visible in lineage, so failures are traced to the right layer; version-controlled seeds mean reference data is deterministic and cannot silently drift, making builds reproducible.

coreComponents.name: Source declarations (sources YAML)
coreComponents.definition: A YAML file with version: 2 and a top-level 'sources' key listing each source's logical name, database, schema, and tables; it registers raw warehouse tables so models can reference them.
coreComponents.purpose: To give already-loaded raw tables an explicit, environment-portable identity that models reference by name rather than by hard-coded relation.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Map a logical source name to a physical database/schema, list the raw tables, and optionally carry descriptions, tests, and freshness config.
coreComponents.examples: sources: - name: raw / database: analytics_db / schema: raw / tables: - name: orders

coreComponents.name: The source() and ref() functions
coreComponents.definition: {{ source('raw','orders') }} resolves to the declared raw table and adds a source dependency edge; {{ ref('country_codes') }} resolves a model or seed name to its warehouse relation and adds a dependency edge.
coreComponents.purpose: To let model SQL point at raw data (source) and at seeds/models (ref) without hard-coding names, feeding dbt's DAG and lineage.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Translate logical names into fully qualified relations at compile time and declare dependencies so dbt builds things in the right order.

coreComponents.name: Seeds (CSV files + dbt seed)
coreComponents.definition: Static CSV files in the seeds/ directory that 'dbt seed' loads into the warehouse as tables; column types can be configured, and each seed is referenced via ref().
coreComponents.purpose: To version-control and load small, static reference/lookup data alongside transformation code.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store small mapping/reference data in the repo, define column types when needed, and materialize as a queryable table on 'dbt seed'.

internalWorking: When dbt parses the project, it reads every YAML file: any file with a top-level 'sources' key registers source nodes, mapping each logical source.table to a physical database.schema.table for the active target/environment.

During compilation, {{ source('raw','orders') }} is replaced with the fully qualified relation (e.g. analytics_db.raw.orders) and a source->model edge is added to the DAG; the source itself is a green node at the top of lineage that dbt never builds, only reads.

For freshness, dbt runs a query against the source table's loaded_at_field, computes the age of the newest record, and compares it to warn_after/error_after thresholds, emitting a warn or error status per source without touching your models.

For seeds, 'dbt seed' reads each CSV in seeds/, infers or applies configured column_types, and issues CREATE TABLE + INSERT (or the adapter's bulk-load equivalent) to materialize the CSV as a warehouse table in the project's target schema.

Once loaded, a seed is indistinguishable from a model to downstream SQL: {{ ref('country_codes') }} resolves to that table and adds a dependency edge, so dbt builds/loads the seed before any model that references it.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Ingestion tool loads raw tables -> sources YAML declares them -> {{ source() }} in staging models -> DAG (source nodes -> models) | seeds/*.csv -> dbt seed loads to warehouse -> {{ ref('seed') }} in models -> compiled SQL -> warehouse executes -> tested, documented models -> BI consumers
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. Fivetran (or another loader) lands raw.orders and raw.customers into the warehouse; dbt does not load these - it only points at them.
2. A sources YAML file declares source 'raw' with database/schema and lists orders and customers, and adds a freshness block (loaded_at_field: _loaded_at, warn_after 12h, error_after 24h).
3. A small country_codes.csv is committed to seeds/ and loaded with 'dbt seed', creating an analytics.country_codes table used to map ISO codes to country names.
4. A staging model selects from {{ source('raw','orders') }} and joins {{ ref('country_codes') }}, so dbt records both a source edge and a seed edge in the DAG.
5. 'dbt source freshness' runs first to confirm raw data is current; if fresh, 'dbt build' loads the seed, builds staging then marts in order, and the results flow to BI dashboards.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named declaration of raw tables that already exist in the warehouse, referenced via {{ source('name','table') }} and never built by dbt.
keyTerminology.importance: Sources decouple models from physical raw names, make the raw layer explicit in lineage, and enable freshness testing of upstream loads.

keyTerminology.meaning: A check comparing the newest loaded_at_field timestamp in a source table against warn_after/error_after thresholds to detect stale upstream data.
keyTerminology.importance: It catches broken or delayed ingestion before models build on stale data, preventing dashboards from silently showing out-of-date numbers.

keyTerminology.meaning: A small static CSV file in the seeds/ directory that 'dbt seed' loads into the warehouse as a table, referenced with {{ ref('seed_name') }}.
keyTerminology.importance: Seeds keep small reference/lookup data version-controlled with the code so it is reviewed, reproducible, and consistent across environments.

keyTerminology.meaning: The column in a source table (often a load timestamp like _loaded_at) that freshness checks use to measure how recently data arrived.
keyTerminology.importance: Without a correct loaded_at_field, freshness cannot be computed, so choosing the right timestamp column is essential for meaningful staleness alerts.

importantConcepts.explanation: What: a source maps a logical name (raw.orders) to a physical relation, so models say {{ source('raw','orders') }} instead of analytics_db.raw.orders. Why: raw table locations differ per environment (dev vs prod) and can be renamed by loaders; hard-coding them scatters brittle references across models. How: change the database/schema once in the sources YAML and every model re-points automatically at compile time. Pitfall: selecting directly from a raw relation (from raw.orders) bypasses the source, breaking lineage and freshness and making promotion between environments fail with 'relation not found'.

importantConcepts.concept: Sources vs seeds - external data vs repo data
importantConcepts.explanation: What: sources point at data loaded into the warehouse by someone else; seeds are CSVs that live in your dbt repo and dbt loads. Why: they serve opposite needs - large, changing operational data (sources) versus small, static, hand-curated reference data (seeds). How: declare sources in YAML and reference with source(); commit CSVs to seeds/, run 'dbt seed', and reference with ref(). Pitfall: using a seed for large or frequently-changing data - seeds are loaded row-by-row via INSERTs, are slow and git-bloating at scale, and are not meant to replace an ingestion pipeline.

What: 'dbt source freshness' measures how old the newest row in each source is and returns pass/warn/error. Why: models built on stale raw data produce stale metrics that look current, which is worse than an obvious outage. How: set loaded_at_field and warn_after/error_after per source, run the freshness command in your schedule before 'dbt build', and alert on error status. Pitfall: pointing loaded_at_field at a business timestamp (e.g. order_date) instead of a load timestamp measures when events happened, not when data arrived, giving misleading freshness.

variationsAndTypes: **Sources (external raw data):** declared in YAML, referenced via source(), never built by dbt - the raw layer of the DAG.
**Source freshness:** optional per-source or per-table config (loaded_at_field, warn_after, error_after) checked with 'dbt source freshness'.
**Seeds (repo CSVs):** static files in seeds/ loaded by 'dbt seed', referenced via ref() - good for country codes, category/status mappings, small lookups.
**Seed configuration:** column_types, quoting, delimiter, and per-seed schema set in dbt_project.yml (or a seed's YAML) to control how the CSV is loaded.
**What NOT to use each for:** sources are not for data dbt should create; seeds are not for large, frequently-changing, or sensitive data (use a source and an ingestion tool instead).
advantages: **Explicit, portable raw layer:** sources map logical names to physical tables, so environment/schema changes are a one-line edit and lineage shows the true raw origin.
**Upstream data-quality gate:** freshness checks detect stale or broken ingestion before models build on bad data.
**Version-controlled reference data:** seeds keep small lookups in git, reviewed and reproducible, identical across all environments.
**Uniform referencing:** both sources and seeds plug into the DAG (via source()/ref()), so dependencies and build order are handled automatically.
disadvantages: **Sources need accurate metadata:** wrong database/schema/loaded_at_field causes 'relation not found' or meaningless freshness results.
**dbt does not load sources:** you still depend on an external ingestion tool and must keep the YAML in sync with reality.
**Seeds do not scale:** loading is row-by-row and slow, and large CSVs bloat the git repo and the seed step.
**Seeds are static:** they only change when someone edits the CSV and re-seeds, so they are unsuitable for data that updates on its own.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Declare a source for any raw table loaded into the warehouse by an ingestion tool, and add freshness where staleness would mislead. Use a seed for small (roughly under a few thousand rows), static, hand-curated reference data - lookup/mapping tables, code-to-label dictionaries - that belongs in version control.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Do not use a seed for large, frequently-changing, or sensitive/PII data, or as a substitute for a real ingestion pipeline. Do not use a source for data dbt itself creates (that is a model or seed), and avoid pointing loaded_at_field at a business timestamp when you mean load time.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Your warehouse is a professional kitchen. Sources are ingredients a supplier delivers and stocks in the walk-in fridge - dbt does not deliver them, it just posts a labeled map ('raw orders, shelf 3') so recipes can find them by name, and a freshness check is the cook sniffing the milk to confirm it has not expired before using it. Seeds are the small jars of house-made spice blends the kitchen keeps in its own labeled cupboard and records in the recipe binder (git): tiny, curated, and versioned. When you write 'dbt seed', you are placing those jars on the shelf so recipes can reach for them exactly like any prepared ingredient.

commonMisconceptions.myth: dbt loads or extracts the data behind a source.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A source is only a declaration pointing at tables an ingestion tool already loaded. dbt never populates a source - it just resolves the name and, optionally, checks how fresh the data is. Extraction and loading are someone else's job.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Seeds are a good way to load any static or reference data, regardless of size.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Seeds are for small data only. They are loaded via INSERT-style statements, which are slow for large files, and the CSV lives in git, bloating the repo. For anything sizeable or frequently changing, use a source loaded by an ingestion tool.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You reference a seed with {{ source() }} because it is 'input' data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Seeds are referenced with {{ ref('seed_name') }}, exactly like a model - dbt builds/loads them and owns them. {{ source() }} is only for externally loaded raw tables that dbt does not create.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Reuse a single source declaration across many models and keep seeds tiny; for large reference data switch to a source loaded by an ingestion tool, since seeds load row-by-row and do not scale.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Run 'dbt source freshness' on a schedule before builds so stale upstream data is caught early; version-control seeds so reference data is deterministic and reproducible across runs.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Treat freshness errors as a gate that halts or delays the build so models are not constructed on stale data; because sources are declarations, a re-point is a safe YAML change with no data movement.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Capture sources.json from freshness runs and track per-source pass/warn/error status and last-loaded age; alert when any source enters error state, signaling a broken ingestion job.
productionConsiderations.security: Keep sensitive raw data as warehouse sources governed by role-based access, never as seed CSVs in git; seeds should hold only non-sensitive reference data since they are stored in the repository.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Use freshness to skip builds when upstream data has not changed, avoiding wasted warehouse compute; keep seeds small so the seed step stays cheap and fast.
productionConsiderations.performance: Set explicit column_types on seeds to avoid mis-inferred wide types that slow joins; declare sources at the right granularity so lineage and freshness queries stay simple and quick.

codeExamples.title: Declaring sources with freshness (sources YAML)
codeExamples.overview: A version: 2 YAML file that registers raw tables as a dbt source and configures freshness thresholds so dbt can warn or error when data is stale.
codeExamples.code:
# models/staging/_sources.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: raw                     # logical name used in {{ source('raw', ...) }}
    database: analytics_db        # where the loaded raw data lives
    schema: raw
    # default freshness for every table in this source
    loaded_at_field: _loaded_at   # a LOAD timestamp column, not a business date
    freshness:
      warn_after:  { count: 12, period: hour }
      error_after: { count: 24, period: hour }
    tables:
      - name: orders
        description: "Raw orders as landed by Fivetran."
      - name: customers
        # this table overrides the source-level freshness
        freshness:
          warn_after: { count: 6, period: hour }
          error_after: { count: 12, period: hour }
codeExamples.breakdown: version: 2 is mandatory or dbt rejects the file. The source 'raw' maps to database analytics_db, schema raw; the name 'raw' is what you pass to source(). loaded_at_field and the freshness block apply to all tables unless a table overrides them - customers here uses tighter thresholds. Descriptions surface in dbt docs. Nothing here is built by dbt; it only declares and (optionally) freshness-checks existing tables.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: dbt now recognizes source('raw','orders') and source('raw','customers'); both appear as green source nodes at the top of the lineage graph, and 'dbt source freshness' can be run against them.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Omitting 'version: 2' makes dbt reject the file. A wrong database/schema causes 'relation not found' at run time. Pointing loaded_at_field at a business date (order_date) instead of a load timestamp gives misleading freshness.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set freshness at the source level and override only where needed; group tables by ingestion system so one broken loader maps to one source in alerts.

codeExamples.title: Using source() and a seed via ref() in a model
codeExamples.overview: A staging model that reads a declared raw source and joins a version-controlled seed to enrich orders with country names.
codeExamples.code:
-- models/staging/stg_orders_enriched.sql
{{ config(materialized='view') }}

select
    o.id                     as order_id,
    o.customer_id,
    lower(o.status)          as status,
    o.amount_cents / 100.0   as order_amount,
    cc.country_name
from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}      as o        -- externally loaded raw table
left join {{ ref('country_codes') }}    as cc        -- a seed CSV in the repo
    on o.country_code = cc.country_code
where o.status is not null
codeExamples.breakdown: {{ source('raw','orders') }} compiles to the fully qualified raw table (e.g. analytics_db.raw.orders) and adds a source dependency. {{ ref('country_codes') }} resolves to the seed table dbt loaded and adds a seed dependency, so dbt loads the seed before building this model. The result is a clean view joining raw orders to a curated code-to-name mapping - a classic use of a seed for a small lookup.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: After 'dbt seed' and 'dbt run', the warehouse has a view analytics.stg_orders_enriched with columns order_id, customer_id, status, order_amount, country_name.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Referencing the seed with {{ source('country_codes') }} fails - seeds use ref(). Selecting 'from raw.orders' directly bypasses the source and breaks lineage/freshness. Forgetting to run 'dbt seed' first means country_codes does not exist yet.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep the seed small and set country_code as a text type in config so the join key does not mis-infer as an integer; materialize enrichment as a view since it is light logic.

codeExamples.title: Loading seeds and checking freshness from the CLI
codeExamples.overview: The command-line workflow: configure seed column types, load seeds, run a freshness check, then build.
codeExamples.code:
# dbt_project.yml (excerpt) - control how a seed CSV loads
seeds:
  my_project:
    country_codes:
      +column_types:
        country_code: varchar(2)
        country_name: varchar(100)

# --- CLI ---------------------------------------------------
# Load all CSVs in seeds/ into the warehouse as tables
dbt seed

# Load just one seed
dbt seed --select country_codes

# Check how fresh each declared source is (writes target/sources.json)
dbt source freshness

# Build models + tests in DAG order (seeds already loaded)
dbt build
codeExamples.breakdown: The dbt_project.yml seeds block pins column_types so country_code loads as varchar(2) instead of an inferred type - important for reliable joins. 'dbt seed' materializes every CSV; '--select' narrows to one. 'dbt source freshness' queries each source's loaded_at_field and records pass/warn/error to sources.json. 'dbt build' then runs models and tests in dependency order.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ dbt seed
16:20:03  Running with dbt=1.9.0
16:20:03  Found 1 seed, 2 sources
16:20:05  1 of 1 OK loaded seed file analytics.country_codes ... [INSERT 249 in 1.1s]
16:20:05  Completed successfully
16:20:05  Done. PASS=1 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 TOTAL=1

$ dbt source freshness
16:20:12  1 of 2 PASS freshness of raw.orders ................ [PASS in 0.6s]
16:20:13  2 of 2 WARN freshness of raw.customers ............. [WARN in 0.5s]
16:20:13  Done.
codeExamples.commonIssues: A malformed CSV (inconsistent columns, stray quotes) fails the seed load. Omitting column_types can mis-infer a code column as integer, dropping leading zeros. Running 'dbt source freshness' without loaded_at_field configured errors out.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Pin column_types for any code/id column to preserve formatting; run 'dbt source freshness' before 'dbt build' in your schedule and gate the build on it to avoid building on stale data.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce team loads raw orders into Snowflake via Fivetran and needs a trusted daily-revenue-by-country report. They must (a) guarantee the raw data is current before building, and (b) map raw two-letter country codes to readable country names using a small, version-controlled lookup rather than hard-coded CASE statements.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw source: raw.orders (id, customer_id, status, amount_cents, country_code, created_at, _loaded_at) landed hourly by Fivetran. Seed: country_codes.csv committed to seeds/ with columns country_code, country_name (~250 rows).
endToEndExample.architecture: Fivetran does Extract + Load into Snowflake. dbt declares raw as a source with freshness on _loaded_at, loads country_codes.csv as a seed, builds a staging view (stg_orders) reading via source(), then a mart fct_revenue_by_country joining the seed via ref(). Airflow runs 'dbt source freshness' then 'dbt build' on a schedule.
processingSteps: 1. Fivetran loads raw.orders into Snowflake, stamping each row with a _loaded_at timestamp.
2. dbt declares source 'raw' in _sources.yml with loaded_at_field: _loaded_at and warn/error thresholds, and 'dbt source freshness' confirms data is current.
3. country_codes.csv is committed to seeds/ with column_types pinned; 'dbt seed' loads it as analytics.country_codes.
4. stg_orders selects from {{ source('raw','orders') }}, cleaning and casting; fct_revenue_by_country aggregates completed orders and joins {{ ref('country_codes') }} to add country_name.
5. 'dbt build' loads the seed, builds staging then the mart in DAG order, runs tests, and the mart feeds the BI dashboard.
endToEndExample.output: A Snowflake table analytics.fct_revenue_by_country (order_date, country_name, num_orders, total_revenue), rebuilt on schedule, gated by freshness, with country names sourced from a version-controlled seed.
endToEndExample.monitoring: sources.json from freshness runs is tracked so a WARN/ERROR on raw.orders alerts before the build; run_results.json records per-model timing and test outcomes; Snowflake query history tracks compute cost.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If freshness returns ERROR (Fivetran stalled), the schedule stops before 'dbt build' so the report is not rebuilt on stale data; if a test on the mart fails, downstream consumers are skipped and the run reruns after the fix.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Leadership gets a daily revenue-by-country report that is guaranteed current (freshness gate) and uses consistent, reviewed country labels (seed), with lineage showing raw source -> staging -> mart and the seed feeding the join.

industryUseCases.problem: Raw orders loaded by an ingestion tool sometimes lagged, causing dashboards to show stale numbers, and country/currency codes were mapped inconsistently across queries.
industryUseCases.solution: Declare raw tables as sources with freshness checks, and store code-to-label mappings as version-controlled seeds referenced via ref().
industryUseCases.benefits: Stale-load alerts before builds and one consistent, reviewed set of lookup mappings shared by every model.

industryUseCases.problem: Reporting needed small reference tables (account-type codes, region groupings, fee schedules) that changed rarely but had to be auditable and consistent across environments.
industryUseCases.solution: Keep those reference tables as seed CSVs in the dbt repo so changes go through code review and load identically in dev and prod.
industryUseCases.benefits: Auditable, reproducible reference data with a git history, no manual warehouse edits, and identical behavior across environments.

industryUseCases.problem: Many staging models selected directly from raw schemas by hard-coded name, so promoting a project to a new environment or renamed schema broke dozens of models at once.
industryUseCases.solution: Introduce source declarations so all raw references go through {{ source() }}, making environment re-points a single YAML change.
industryUseCases.benefits: Portable projects, correct lineage of the raw layer, and the ability to add freshness tests to every upstream table.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Sources scale for free since they are declarations reused across models; seeds do not scale (row-by-row loads, git storage), so reference data that grows should migrate to a source loaded by an ingestion tool.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Freshness checks gate builds so stale upstream data cannot silently propagate; because sources move no data, re-pointing a source to a new schema is a safe, instantaneous YAML change with no risk of partial loads.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Availability of raw data rests on the ingestion tool and the managed warehouse; dbt sources are stateless declarations and seeds are reproducible from the repo, so a rebuilt project can recreate seeds anywhere.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Seeds are recoverable from git and reloadable with 'dbt seed'; sources point at immutable raw tables, so the full transformed layer can be rebuilt from retained raw data plus the versioned seed CSVs.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Pin seed column_types to avoid wide mis-inferred types that slow joins; declare sources at sensible granularity so freshness queries stay simple, and run freshness only on tables where staleness matters.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Use freshness to skip rebuilds when upstream data is unchanged, saving warehouse compute; keep seeds tiny so the seed step is negligible, and avoid loading large data as seeds where an ingestion tool is cheaper.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Never store sensitive/PII data as seed CSVs in git; keep such data as warehouse sources governed by role-based access. Seeds should contain only non-sensitive reference data, and warehouse credentials stay in secrets, not code.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Ingest sources.json (freshness) and run_results.json into monitoring; track last-loaded age per source, seed load timing, and alert on any source in error state to catch broken ingestion early.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Add tests to sources (not_null, unique, relationships) and seeds just like models, and use freshness as a first-class data-quality check so stale raw data fails the pipeline before it reaches consumers.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: dbt logs each seed load and freshness result; wire the orchestrator to alert on freshness ERROR, seed load failures, and source test failures, surfacing stale or malformed upstream data promptly.

recommendedPractices: **Declare every raw table as a source** and reference it with {{ source() }} - never select from a raw relation by hard-coded name.
**Add freshness checks** (loaded_at_field + warn_after/error_after) to sources where stale data would mislead, and run them before builds.
**Use seeds only for small, static reference data** (codes, mappings) and reference them with {{ ref() }}.
**Pin seed column_types** for code/id columns so leading zeros and formats are preserved and joins are reliable.
engineeringStandards: Keep a version: 2 sources YAML per ingestion system and keep its database/schema in sync with the actual loaded location per environment.
Version-control all seed CSVs and require code review for changes to reference data.
Point loaded_at_field at a genuine load timestamp, never a business date, so freshness measures data arrival.
designRecommendations: Group source tables by the system/loader that produces them so alerts map cleanly to one broken pipeline.
Prefer a source over a seed for anything that changes on its own or exceeds a few thousand rows.
Keep raw immutable: never transform in the source declaration - do all cleaning in staging models.
namingConventions: Name sources after the source system/schema (e.g. 'raw', 'stripe', 'salesforce') so {{ source('stripe','charges') }} reads clearly.
Give seeds descriptive, snake_case names of the lookup they hold (country_codes, category_mapping, status_labels).
Match seed CSV column headers to the snake_case column names you want in the warehouse.
documentationStandards: Describe each source and its key tables/columns in YAML so dbt docs shows a useful raw-layer catalog.
Document what each seed maps and who owns updates to it, since reference data drifts if unowned.
Note freshness thresholds and their rationale (e.g. 'hourly load, warn at 12h') alongside the source.
testingStrategies: Run 'dbt source freshness' on a schedule and gate builds on it so stale raw data stops the pipeline.
Add generic tests (not_null, unique, relationships) to source tables and to seed key columns.
Test that seed lookups cover expected keys (e.g. a relationships test from staging.country_code to the seed).

commonMistakes.mistake: Selecting directly from a raw table (from raw.orders) instead of declaring and using a source.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is the fastest way to get a query running, and analysts write SQL the way they always have.
commonMistakes.impact: Broken lineage (the raw layer is invisible), no freshness checks, and models that fail with 'relation not found' when promoted to another environment.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Declare the raw table as a source in a version: 2 YAML and reference it with {{ source('raw','orders') }} so lineage, portability, and freshness all work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a seed to load large or frequently-changing data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Seeds are easy - drop a CSV in seeds/ and run 'dbt seed' - so they get misused as a general loading mechanism.
commonMistakes.impact: Slow row-by-row loads, a bloated git repo, and stale data because seeds only change when someone edits the CSV and re-seeds.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Reserve seeds for small, static reference data; for large or auto-updating data, load it with an ingestion tool and declare it as a source.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting loaded_at_field to a business timestamp instead of a load timestamp.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Business dates like order_date or created_at are the obvious timestamp columns and are mistaken for freshness signals.
commonMistakes.impact: Freshness measures when events happened, not when data arrived, so a broken loader can still report 'fresh' and stale data reaches dashboards.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use a genuine load/ingestion timestamp (e.g. _loaded_at added by the loader) as loaded_at_field so freshness reflects data arrival.

comparisonSection.explanation: A source points at data an ingestion tool already loaded into the warehouse; dbt never creates it and only declares/optionally freshness-checks it, referencing it with {{ source() }}. A seed is a CSV that lives in the dbt repo, is loaded by 'dbt seed', and is owned by the project, referenced with {{ ref() }}. Use sources for large, changing operational data and seeds for small, static, version-controlled reference data.

comparisonSection.optionA: Source (any size, changes on its own)
comparisonSection.explanation: Sources handle arbitrarily large tables that refresh continuously via the loader, and freshness tracks how current they are. Seeds are loaded row-by-row from a committed CSV, so they suit only small tables (roughly a few thousand rows) that change rarely and by hand. Loading large or frequently-changing data as a seed is slow, bloats git, and goes stale - that data belongs in a source.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a dbt source and how do you reference it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A source is a declaration, in a version: 2 YAML file under the 'sources' key, that names raw tables already loaded into the warehouse (with their database and schema). You reference it in models with {{ source('source_name', 'table_name') }}, which resolves to the fully qualified table name and adds a dependency edge to the DAG. dbt never builds a source - it only points at it.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that dbt does not load sources and that source() both resolves the name and creates lineage. Mention that it decouples models from physical raw table names for portability.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a seed in dbt and when should you use one?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A seed is a small static CSV file in the seeds/ directory that dbt loads into the warehouse as a table when you run 'dbt seed'; you reference it with {{ ref('seed_name') }}. Use seeds for small, static, version-controlled reference data like country codes or category mappings - not for large or frequently-changing data.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the size/static constraint and that seeds are referenced with ref(), not source(), because dbt owns and creates them from the repo.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does source freshness work and how do you configure it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: You set a loaded_at_field (a load timestamp column) plus warn_after and error_after thresholds on a source or table in YAML. Running 'dbt source freshness' queries the newest loaded_at_field value, computes its age, and returns pass/warn/error per source, writing results to sources.json. It never touches your models - it only assesses upstream staleness.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Call out that loaded_at_field must be a load timestamp, not a business date, and that freshness is typically run before 'dbt build' as a data-quality gate.

intermediateQuestions.question: Why use a source() instead of hard-coding the raw table name?
intermediateQuestions.answer: source() decouples model SQL from the physical relation: the database/schema live in one YAML declaration, so changing environments or a renamed schema is a single edit rather than changes across many models. It also makes the raw layer explicit in lineage and enables freshness and source tests. Hard-coding breaks all of that and fails on promotion between environments.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tie it to portability (dev vs prod) and lineage; a strong answer mentions that source() also adds the source node to the DAG.

advancedQuestions.question: When would a seed be the wrong choice, and what do you use instead?
advancedQuestions.answer: A seed is wrong for large, frequently-changing, or sensitive data. Seeds load row-by-row (slow at scale), store the CSV in git (repo bloat and PII risk), and only update when someone edits and re-seeds (stale). For large or auto-updating data, load it with an ingestion tool and declare it as a source; for sensitive data, keep it in the warehouse under role-based access as a source.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you understand seeds' mechanics (INSERT-style loads, git storage) and the security angle (no PII in git). The alternative is always a source plus an ingestion pipeline.

advancedQuestions.question: How do sources and seeds appear in the DAG, and how does that affect build order?
advancedQuestions.answer: Sources are terminal upstream nodes that dbt reads but never builds; a {{ source() }} adds a source->model edge so the model knows its raw origin. Seeds are buildable nodes loaded by 'dbt seed'; a {{ ref('seed') }} adds a seed->model edge, so dbt loads the seed before any model that references it. Both feed the same dependency graph that dbt uses to order and parallelize the run.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Distinguish that sources are never built while seeds are loaded, but both create dependency edges. This shows understanding of how the DAG treats each node type.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your daily dashboard occasionally shows yesterday's numbers as if current because Fivetran silently stalled overnight, and separately, three analysts hard-code different country-code-to-name mappings. How do you fix both with dbt?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The stale-data issue is an upstream freshness problem - declare the raw table as a source with loaded_at_field and thresholds, and gate the build on 'dbt source freshness'. The inconsistent mapping is duplicated reference data - centralize it as a version-controlled seed referenced via ref() and have all models join that one table.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Declare raw.orders as a source with loaded_at_field: _loaded_at and warn/error thresholds; run 'dbt source freshness' before 'dbt build' so a stalled load errors and halts the rebuild. Commit country_codes.csv to seeds/, pin column_types, run 'dbt seed', and refactor all models to join {{ ref('country_codes') }} instead of hard-coded CASE statements. Now data is guaranteed current and country names are consistent and reviewed.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the raw-layer contract for a dbt project that consumes data from three ingestion systems and needs a handful of small, auditable reference tables.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Create one version: 2 sources YAML per ingestion system, each mapping logical names to the correct database/schema and listing tables, with freshness (loaded_at_field + thresholds) on tables where staleness matters. Store the reference tables as seed CSVs in seeds/ with pinned column_types, referenced via ref(). Run 'dbt source freshness' before 'dbt build' and add source/seed tests.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Sources add YAML maintenance but give portability, lineage, and freshness; seeds give version control and reproducibility for small data but do not scale and must exclude sensitive data. Freshness gating trades a little latency for protection against building on stale data.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Keep sources as the scalable path for growing data; migrate any seed that grows or starts changing to a source loaded by the ingestion tool. Partition sources by system so alerts map to one loader, and run freshness selectively on tables where staleness has business impact.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: dbt sources declare externally loaded raw tables (referenced via source(), with optional freshness checks), while seeds are small version-controlled CSVs that dbt loads into the warehouse and you reference via ref().
keyConcepts: Sources = pointers to raw tables dbt does NOT load; reference with {{ source('name','table') }}.
Seeds = small static CSVs in seeds/ that dbt loads via 'dbt seed'; reference with {{ ref('seed') }}.
Source freshness uses loaded_at_field + warn_after/error_after to detect stale upstream data.
Sources decouple models from physical raw names (portability + lineage); never hard-code raw tables.
Use seeds only for small, static reference data - never for large, changing, or sensitive data.
commands: dbt seed                       # load all CSVs in seeds/ into the warehouse
dbt seed --select country_codes   # load a single seed
dbt source freshness           # check staleness of declared sources
dbt build                      # run seeds + models + tests in DAG order
dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve   # view sources/seeds in lineage
interviewPoints: dbt never loads sources - it only declares and freshness-checks them.
Seeds are referenced with ref(), sources with source().
loaded_at_field must be a load timestamp, not a business date.
Sources give portability and lineage; seeds give version-controlled reference data.
Seeds do not scale: row-by-row loads and git storage - keep them tiny.
quickNotes: Both sources and seeds YAML start with 'version: 2'.
Set freshness at source level; override per table where needed.
Pin seed +column_types (e.g. varchar) to preserve codes/leading zeros.
Run 'dbt source freshness' before 'dbt build' as a data-quality gate.
Never put PII in a seed CSV - keep sensitive data as a warehouse source.

keyTakeaways: Sources declare raw tables that already exist in the warehouse (loaded by an ingestion tool); dbt never populates them - it only resolves {{ source('name','table') }} to the real relation and adds it to the DAG.
Declaring sources decouples model SQL from physical raw table names, so environment or schema changes are a one-line YAML edit, and the raw layer becomes explicit in lineage and testable.
Source freshness (loaded_at_field + warn_after/error_after, run with 'dbt source freshness') is a data-quality gate that catches stale or broken upstream loads before models build on bad data.

Seeds are small static CSVs in seeds/ that 'dbt seed' loads into the warehouse and you reference with {{ ref('seed') }}; they are ideal for version-controlled reference/lookup data like country codes and category mappings.

The core rule: sources are for external raw data (any size, loaded by others) while seeds are for small, static, repo-owned reference data - never use a seed for large, frequently-changing, or sensitive data.
